solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: The estate is run down, people say

indicators.note: what people say is heard rather than read, so the sound of the phrase before it counts, not its spelling

blocks.note: to run someone down is to demean them

explanation.surface: A neglected country estate falling into disrepair, as the locals report.
explanation.walkthrough: DEMESNE is pronounced like DEMEAN; the odd spelling with S is the giveaway once you know the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A demesne is the land attached to a manor house, kept for the owner's own use: a landed property.

clue.text: Foolish to make Pinky or Perky “discontented”

indicators.note: with its contents emptied out, a word keeps only its shell of first and last letters

blocks.note: to make a cake is to do one
either name begins with P and ends with Y

explanation.surface: A jibe that the puppet pigs Pinky and Perky would look silly if they were made unhappy.
explanation.walkthrough: Pinky and Perky were puppet pigs on British TV in the 1950s and 60s; the quotation marks warn that 'discontented' is meant literally, contents removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Dopy is an informal adjective for slow-witted or stupid, a straightforward synonym for silly behaviour.

clue.text: European in Webster’s play setting, cold and evil

indicators.note: one thing set in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: John Webster's tragedy is The Duchess of Malfi, set in that Italian town
E is the abbreviation for European
C for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A description of the chilly, wicked atmosphere of Webster's Jacobean revenge tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suits Webster's famously dark play, which hides that 'evil' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Malefic is a literary adjective meaning causing harm or wickedness, a formal synonym for malign.

clue.text: Given errand to collect pennies, to be this?

definitions.text: Given errand to collect pennies, to be this?

indicators.note: collecting something means gathering it in and holding it inside

blocks.note: someone given an errand is sent on it
p is the abbreviation for pennies, as in 50p

explanation.surface: Wondering whether being sent out to fetch coins leaves you worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: after running an errand to gather money, you might be exhausted, or the money might be paid out.
explanation.definitionFit: Spent means exhausted after effort, and also describes money already paid out, both fitting the errand scenario.

clue.text: Fullness of being, about to be limited

indicators.note: something limited is hemmed in by boundaries on either side

blocks.note: a being is an entity
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A philosophical musing that the full richness of existence is about to be curtailed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fullness of being' reads as one phrase, but 'of' is the link and 'being' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Entirety is the state of being whole and complete, the same idea as total fullness.

clue.text: Register a line, one ignored by enthusiast

indicators.note: if something is ignored by a word, that word carries on without it, so it drops out

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for line
a maniac for something is a fanatical fan
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Recording a line in a register, with one entry overlooked by an eager hobbyist.
explanation.definitionFit: An almanac is an annual publication listing dates and data, a kind of calendar or register of events.

clue.text: Sudden power to punch a bully no end

indicators.note: with no end, a word loses its final letter
a punch drives into something, so this goes inside the other piece

blocks.note: taken as written
a bully is a brute
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: A sudden burst of strength used to land a punch on a never-ending bully.
explanation.walkthrough: BRUTE loses its last letter to give BRUT, and P goes inside it before the T.
explanation.definitionFit: Abrupt means happening suddenly and without warning, a direct adjective synonym for sudden.

clue.text: Old Democrat organised procession for head of state?

indicators.note: organising means putting into a new order, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
taken as written

explanation.surface: A veteran Democratic politician arranging a parade for a president.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' looks like it describes the Democrat, but it supplies an extra letter for the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorcade is a procession of cars, typically escorting a president or visiting dignitary, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Bulletins about horse in training those my sister gave me?

indicators.note: about means around, so one word wraps the other
one thing in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: news bulletins
PE is physical education, or physical training at school
H is slang for heroin, known as horse

explanation.surface: News reports about a racehorse being trained, set beside a family puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: Horse is old slang for heroin, abbreviated H; the double insertion builds from the inside out.
explanation.definitionFit: A sister's sons are her sibling's nephews, so these are the relatives she gave her brother or sister.

clue.text: Take advantage of what Italy and Israel are said to need

indicators.note: something said is spoken, so the spoken phrase counts rather than how it is spelt

blocks.note: both names start with an upper-case letter I

explanation.surface: Exploiting what two Mediterranean countries require, perhaps funding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' suggests money or capital cities, but it is the upper-case letter each country name starts with.
explanation.definitionFit: To capitalise on something is to exploit an opportunity or turn it to your benefit.

clue.text: Material that could be adapted to poet’s lyre

indicators.note: adapting something changes its form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A fabric that might be fitted to a poet's stringed instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: Polyester is a synthetic fibre and the cloth woven from it, a type of fabric.

clue.text: Seal dedication? Add a little

blocks.note: a dedication begins 'To ...', as in 'To my mother'
a young seal is a pup

explanation.surface: A wordless hint that a seal's devotion could be enhanced a bit.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces appear in the clue in reverse order: the dedication word comes first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To top up is to add a small quantity to fill something back up, like a drink or a phone balance.

clue.text: Tense with highly optimistic hope

blocks.note: first meaning: the grammatical tense of 'will have done'
second meaning: a wish that what lies ahead will be flawless

explanation.surface: Someone anxious yet clinging to wildly rosy expectations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' reads as nervous, but it is the grammar term.
explanation.definitionFit: It names the verb form for actions completed by a later time, and literally a flawless time to come.

clue.text: Space traveller circling orbit extremely eager for a measure of applause

indicators.note: circling something means going all round it, so one piece surrounds the other
the extremes of a word are its very first and very last letters

blocks.note: a comet travels through space
one orbit of a track or planet is a lap
first and last letters of eager

explanation.surface: An astronaut keen to go round the earth again, oddly tied to measuring applause.
explanation.walkthrough: A clapometer was the dial on TV talent shows such as Opportunity Knocks that showed how loudly the studio audience clapped.
explanation.definitionFit: A clapometer is a device, often comic, that gauges the volume of clapping from an audience.

clue.text: Gash tree, the outside being dead

indicators.note: what forms the outside wraps around the other piece

blocks.note: the late king is the dead king
acer is the maple genus

explanation.surface: Cutting into a tree whose bark has died.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gash tree' reads as an instruction to cut a tree, but 'Gash' is the verb definition alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To lacerate is to tear or cut flesh deeply, the same as inflicting a gash as a verb.

clue.text: With nothing in store, safer bet to cook this?

definitions.text: With nothing in store, safer bet to cook this?

indicators.note: cooking letters means mixing them up into something new
what is in store is kept inside, so this piece goes within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: With an empty larder, a reliable joint is the safest thing to make.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of SAFER BET gets O inside it after its first letter. The whole clue also serves as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Roast beef is a classic Sunday dinner, a dependable dish to cook when you have nothing else in.

clue.text: Woman left to collect son and daughter perhaps

indicators.note: collecting means gathering in, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: a dame is a woman
L for left
S for son, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: A mother leaving to pick up her son and daughter from school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woman' looks like the definition, but it is wordplay; the definition is at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A damsel is an archaic word for a young unmarried woman, which a daughter might be.

clue.text: Stop working to steal

blocks.note: first meaning: to finish for the day
second meaning: slang for pinching something

explanation.surface: Quitting your job in order to turn thief.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to end the working day and, informally, to pilfer goods.

clue.text: Was obliged to return after almost perfect seclusion

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
returning means going back the way it came, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: perfect, unblemished: pure
'had to' means was obliged to

explanation.surface: Someone forced to come back after a nearly flawless period of isolation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the reversed piece second, following the shortened PURE.
explanation.definitionFit: Purdah is the practice of screening women from public view, and by extension any state of isolation.

clue.text: Indistinct muttering right over pub in centre

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: R for right
a hub is a centre
a bar is a pub

explanation.surface: Mumbling heard in a pub in town.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts R on top of the rest. Actors say the word repeatedly to make background crowd noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhubarb is the noise actors make to suggest a murmuring crowd, hence any unintelligible background chatter.

clue.text: Spooks: headless horses in race round village boundaries

indicators.note: with its head removed, a word loses its first letter
the boundaries of a word are its outermost letters
going round something means surrounding it

blocks.note: horses in a race are runners
first and last letters of village

explanation.surface: Ghostly headless horsemen racing around a village, like Sleepy Hollow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spooks' reads as ghosts, but here it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To spook someone is to frighten or unsettle them, which is what unnerves means as a verb.

clue.text: Lead and uranium atomic team use principally in remote islands

indicators.note: principally means chiefly or first, so each word gives its opening letter

blocks.note: the van is the lead position, as in vanguard
U is the chemical symbol for uranium
the first letters of atomic, team and use

explanation.surface: Nuclear materials used by scientists on far-flung islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' looks like the chemical element beside uranium, but it means being in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Vanuatu is a Pacific island nation of about eighty islands, far from any continent.

clue.text: Unreasonable influences one found in headquarters

indicators.note: something found in a place is inside it

blocks.note: headquarters are bases
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Unfair pressures detected at the head office.
explanation.definitionFit: Biases are prejudices that sway judgement unfairly, plural nouns matching the plural phrase.

clue.text: Range of human action involved at home

indicators.note: something involved is tangled and complicated, so the letters are mixed

blocks.note: taken as written
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: The scope of what people do when they stay at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Range of' reads as 'variety of', but 'Range' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A mountain range is a linked series of peaks, also called a chain.

clue.text: Anger unknown by a revolutionary Eurasian

indicators.note: a revolution turns something round, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: ire is anger
in algebra x, y and z are unknowns
taken as written

explanation.surface: A furious, obscure rebel from somewhere between Europe and Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: An Azeri is a person from Azerbaijan, a country straddling the border of Europe and Asia.

clue.text: Opponent eating large ice

indicators.note: eating something takes it inside

blocks.note: an opponent is a foe
L for large, as on clothing

explanation.surface: A rival tucking into a big ice cream.
explanation.definitionFit: A floe is a sheet of floating sea ice, so a specific kind of the frozen stuff.

clue.text: Suspicion online basket has been withdrawn

indicators.note: something withdrawn is pulled back, so the word is read in the backward direction

blocks.note: an online shopping basket is an e-cart

explanation.surface: A shopper suspecting that their web shopping basket was cancelled.
explanation.definitionFit: A suspicion can mean a tiny amount or hint, as in a suspicion of garlic, which is a trace.

clue.text: Be defensive — the way a single wicket is followed by the rest

blocks.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
a single is one
W is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for wicket
all the rest, everything remaining

explanation.surface: A cricket picture: one wicket falls and then the rest of the batting side collapses.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a batter who stonewalls blocks every ball rather than trying to score.
explanation.definitionFit: To stonewall is to stall or block persistently, playing purely defensively in cricket or in argument.

clue.text: Snubs English bishop wearing frills

indicators.note: what is worn goes around the wearer, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: ruffs are frilled collars
E for English
B for bishop in chess notation

explanation.surface: An English cleric in fancy collars cold-shouldering people.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebuff is a blunt rejection, so rebuffs as a verb means rejects or cold-shoulders someone.

clue.text: Footballers getting one draw and a defeat

blocks.note: the FA is the Football Association, England's governing body
Roman numeral one
to draw in is to lure

explanation.surface: A team's poor run of results: a draw and then a loss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw' suggests a tied match, but it is a verb meaning attract.
explanation.definitionFit: A failure is an unsuccessful outcome, so a defeat counts as one, both being nouns with an article.
